import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 1071

*References:*
* [erdosproblems.com/1071](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1071)
* [Da85] Danzer, L., _Some combinatorial and metric problems in geometry_.
  Intuitive geometry (Siófok, 1985), 167-177.
-/

open Set Metric EuclideanGeometry Order

namespace Erdos1071

/-- Two segments are disjoint if they only intersect at their endpoints (if at all). -/
def SegmentsDisjoint (seg1 seg2 : ℝ² × ℝ²) : Prop :=
  segment ℝ seg1.1 seg1.2 ∩ segment ℝ seg2.1 seg2.2 ⊆ {seg1.1, seg1.2, seg2.1, seg2.2}

/--
Can a finite set of disjoint unit segments in a unit square be maximal?
Solved affirmatively by [Da85], who gave an explicit construction.

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle and ChatGPT.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 52, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos1071.lean"]
theorem erdos_1071.parts.i :
    answer(True) ↔ ∃ S : Finset (ℝ² × ℝ²),
      Maximal (fun T : Finset (ℝ² × ℝ²) =>
        (∀ seg ∈ T, dist seg.1 seg.2 = 1 ∧
          seg.1 0 ∈ Icc 0 1 ∧ seg.1 1 ∈ Icc 0 1 ∧
          seg.2 0 ∈ Icc 0 1 ∧ seg.2 1 ∈ Icc 0 1) ∧
          (T : Set (ℝ² × ℝ²)).Pairwise SegmentsDisjoint) S := by
  sorry

/-- Is there a region $R$ with a maximal set of disjoint unit line segments that is countably infinite?
Solved affirmatively by [Fo99], who gave an explicit construction.

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle and ChatGPT.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 52, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos1071b.lean"]
theorem erdos_1071.parts.ii :
    answer(True) ↔ ∃ (R : Set ℝ²) (S : Set (ℝ² × ℝ²)),
      IsOpen R ∧ IsConnected R ∧ S.Countable ∧ S.Infinite ∧
      Maximal (fun T : Set (ℝ² × ℝ²) =>
        (∀ seg ∈ T, dist seg.1 seg.2 = 1 ∧ seg.1 ∈ R ∧ seg.2 ∈ R) ∧
        T.Pairwise SegmentsDisjoint) S := by
  sorry

end Erdos1071

findings.description: The predicate inside `Maximal` requires only `seg.1 ∈ R ∧ seg.2 ∈ R`, not that the unit interval lies in R. Openness and connectedness do not make R convex. For example, R = ℝ² \ {(0,0)}, a = (-1/2,0), b = (1/2,0) satisfy both topological hypotheses, `dist a b = 1`, and both endpoint-membership conditions, but their open segment contains the excluded origin. This counterexample was proved in Lean. Conversely, a unit open interval can lie in an open region while its endpoints lie on the boundary; the endpoint condition incorrectly excludes those intervals. Thus the declaration changes both admissible families and the extensions considered for maximality.
findings.source_evidence: Erdős, ‘Some combinatorial and metric problems in geometry’ (1987), §7, p.174: ‘Let R be any region and let there be given in R a maximal set of disjoint unit intervals. Can such a set ever be denumerable?’ https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1987-27.pdf. The cited external constructions explicitly define `IsUnitSegment s` using `s = openSegment ℝ x y` and `IsInRegion S R := ∀ s ∈ S, s ⊆ R`. In Erdos1071.lean, `Region_R` is an open rectangle, while the constructed segments have the boundary point `O_point = (0,0)` as an endpoint.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace `dist seg.1 seg.2 = 1 ∧ seg.1 ∈ R ∧ seg.2 ∈ R` with `dist seg.1 seg.2 = 1 ∧ openSegment ℝ seg.1 seg.2 ⊆ R` inside the maximality predicate. Remove, rather than retain, the endpoint-membership requirements, matching the open-unit-interval convention of the cited constructions.

findings.description: The bibliography attributes ‘Some combinatorial and metric problems in geometry’, pp.167–177, to Danzer under `[Da85]`. That paper is by Paul Erdős and was published in 1987. It reports Danzer’s construction from the 1985 meeting; the construction’s attribution is correct, but the publication’s attribution is not.

Erdős, ‘Some combinatorial and metric problems in geometry’, Intuitive geometry (Siófok, 1985), Colloq. Math. Soc. János Bolyai 48, 167–177, North-Holland, 1987. Section 7 credits Danzer with the example. https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1987-27.pdf and https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/Erdos.html.
findings.suggested_fix: Cite the paper as `[Er87b] Erdős, P., ... (1987), 167–177`, and describe part (i) as solved by Danzer at the 1985 meeting, with the construction reported in [Er87b].

reformulations.difference: Uses containment of the intersection of closed segments in the union of their four endpoints instead of directly asserting disjointness of open unit intervals.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For a ≠ b and c ≠ d, a point belongs to both open segments exactly when it belongs to both closed segments and is none of the four endpoints. Consequently the displayed containment is equivalent to `Disjoint (openSegment ℝ a b) (openSegment ℝ c d)`. The unit-distance hypotheses ensure the endpoint inequalities, excluding Mathlib’s degenerate `openSegment a a = {a}` case. The exact equivalence is proved as `disjoint_iff_open` in the scratch file.

reformulations.difference: Tests maximality only against finite families and expresses containment in the square using endpoint coordinate bounds.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The admissibility predicate is hereditary under taking subfamilies. Any proper extension, even an infinite one, supplies a single new segment; inserting it gives a finite proper extension. Thus finite-family maximality is equivalent to maximality among arbitrary families. Also, the closed unit square is convex and closed, so an open segment lies in it iff both endpoints satisfy the stated bounds. These equivalences were proved in Lean as `square_finite_maximal_iff` and `open_in_square_iff_endpoints`. The endpoint test is therefore valid here, unlike for the arbitrary region in part (ii).

demonstrated.claim: The exact admissibility predicate inside Maximal accepts a unit segment whose endpoints lie in an open connected region but whose interior contains a point excluded from that region.

submission.summary: /workspace/review/trivial_proof.lean checks the singleton segment from (-1/2,0) to (1/2,0) in the punctured plane. It demonstrates the incorrect containment hypothesis, without claiming to prove or refute the full existence theorem. Compilation succeeds, and the demonstration depends only on propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound.

trivial_proof.lean:
import FormalConjectures.ErdosProblems.«1071»

/-! A concrete counterexample to the region-containment test in part (ii). -/
open Set Metric EuclideanGeometry

private def p (x : ℝ) : ℝ² := WithLp.toLp 2 ![x, 0]
private def R : Set ℝ² := ({0} : Set ℝ²)ᶜ
private def T : Set (ℝ² × ℝ²) := {(p (-1/2), p (1/2))}

-- Erdos1071.erdos_1071.parts.ii: its predicate inside `Maximal` accepts this
-- singleton, although its unit open segment contains the point omitted from R.
-- This tests the hypothesis as written, not the full existence assertion.
theorem endpoint_admissible_but_not_contained :
    IsOpen R ∧ IsConnected R ∧
      ((∀ seg ∈ T, dist seg.1 seg.2 = 1 ∧ seg.1 ∈ R ∧ seg.2 ∈ R) ∧
        T.Pairwise Erdos1071.SegmentsDisjoint) ∧
      ¬ openSegment ℝ (p (-1/2)) (p (1/2)) ⊆ R := by
  refine ⟨isClosed_singleton.isOpen_compl, ?_, ⟨?_, Set.pairwise_singleton _ _⟩, ?_⟩
  · apply isConnected_compl_singleton_of_one_lt_rank
    rw [← Module.finrank_eq_rank]
    simp
  · intro seg hs
    have hs' : seg = (p (-1/2), p (1/2)) := Set.mem_singleton_iff.mp hs
    subst seg
    refine ⟨?_, ?_, ?_⟩
    · norm_num [p, EuclideanSpace.dist_eq, Fin.sum_univ_two, Real.dist_eq]
    all_goals
      change _ ≠ (0 : ℝ²)
      intro h
      have := congrArg (fun q : ℝ² => q 0) h
      norm_num [p] at this
  · intro h
    have hm : (0 : ℝ²) ∈ openSegment ℝ (p (-1/2)) (p (1/2)) := by
      refine ⟨1/2, 1/2, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, ?_⟩
      ext i
      fin_cases i <;> norm_num [p]
    exact h hm rfl

#print axioms endpoint_admissible_but_not_contained

submission.summary: Replaced endpoint-membership requirements with `openSegment ℝ seg.1 seg.2 ⊆ R` in the maximality predicate. This requires the entire open segment to lie in the region while allowing boundary endpoints. Only the reported containment condition was changed. The required compilation succeeds with only the existing `sorry` warnings.
